articles.title: A Baltimore Warehouse Gives Away Thousands of Free Books Every Year—And Keeps the Love of Reading Circulating
articles.content:
在巴尔的摩市中心北部的一座不起眼的仓库外，每逢第二个周末，人们早早就开始排队。他们带着咖啡、折叠椅和空购物袋，互相打着招呼，等待着"The Book Thing"（书之物）的开放。这里提供免费图书，数量任取——去年就捐赠了超过21.2万本。

“这里的氛围是一种安静的兴奋感。”写作教师拉胡尔·贾卡蒂（Rahul Jakati）这样描述。他第一次拜访后就立刻申请成为志愿者，至今已累计服务超过300小时。在他看来，The Book Thing是巴尔的摩的灵魂之一：“图书在这里不断流入这个‘文学心脏’，再被发送出去，重新激活巴尔的摩的文学生态，这是一种善意的循环。”

The Book Thing始于1995年，当时酒吧老板拉塞尔·瓦滕伯格（Russell Wattenberg）听说当地教师缺乏学生用书，便开始免费赠送。这起源于一桩小小的善举，逐渐成长为巴尔的摩最受欢迎的公益机构之一，传统上每月第二个周末开放。

2017年，一场大火摧毁了部分书库，社区成员纷纷伸出援手，抢救可用书籍。附近的Peabody Heights Brewery甚至腾出货架临时储存书籍，待发放。如今，参观者按预约时间段入场，拥有近一小时的浏览时间。董事会主席克里斯托弗·默根（Christopher Mergen）表示，每月收到的捐赠图书达1.2万至1.7万本，处理起来“堪称一项工程奇迹”。

志愿者们从车厢和卡车上卸下书箱，分类、盖戳“禁止转售”，再按主题分架。书架上有礼仪、奇书、大字本和迷你书等专区。一位女性捐赠了完整的《甜蜜山谷》系列：“这是我青春期的一部分。”她对志愿者说。

“这里的存在本身就是一种奇迹。”默根认为，巴尔的摩向来以迷人特质著称，这里是一个“勤奋自立”的地方。

The Book Thing位于瓦弗利（Waverly）社区，这个地区充满了这种非凡特质。周六，游客们漫步于附近的农贸市场、砖砌排屋、咖啡馆和独立商店之间。周边地区历来注重文学传统。距此不远的埃德加·爱伦·坡故居博物馆是国家历史遗迹；新闻记者H.L.门肯记录了他在巴尔的摩的生活；F·斯科特·菲茨杰拉德也曾在此居住多年。

在一次免费领书日，志愿者欢迎入场的访客，击掌跳舞。一位视障女性随朋友前来，打算在外等待。志愿者发现她后，在媒体专区找到她感兴趣的CD音频书，双方都很欣喜。

另一位女性捐赠了母亲遗留的书籍。当志愿者清点时，她追问这些书是否真的能送到有需要的人手中，随即泪眼婆娑地解释：“知道母亲的书库找到了新家，这意味着太多了。”

巴尔的摩本地人维奥莱特·勒沃伊特（Violet LeVoit）推荐了这家机构：“The Book Thing不偏不倚，所有书籍和人都受到尊重。有时你只是为了乐趣而来，有时寻找特定书籍，有时和同样爱书的朋友交流。在这个万物金钱化的世界里，这里的书和人都是自由的。”

当地英语教师德维娜·巴拉（Devina Bhalla）最难忘的经历并非找到一本好书。她刚搬来时人生地不熟，一位教师同事告诉她这是“巴尔的摩最特别的地方”。于是，The Book Thing成为她最先建立归属感的场所——不仅是对阅读的热爱，更是对这座城市的认同。

她介绍男友科林·肯尼迪（Colin Kennedy）来到这里，两人经常一起光顾。去年一次参观中，他单膝跪地，在书架前向她求婚。认识他们的人都不感到意外。“许多人都说这话，‘Colin在这里求婚，这太合适了’。”

类似的故事让人们不再将The Book Thing视为简单的书库或免费商店，而是友谊、归属感和慷慨的象征。巴拉总结道：“如果有人对人性失望，带他们来这里，证明人类也能做出美好的事。”
articles.summary:
The line begins forming long before the doors open to ­an unassuming warehouse in north-central Baltimore, not far from the Baltimore Museum of Art. People bring coffee. Folding chairs. Empty tote bags. Friends greet one another. They’re waiting for The Book Thing. Free books. As many as you can carry. More than 212,000 given away here last year alone.

“It’s a vibe, I would say, of quiet excitement,” says Rahul Jakati, a writing instructor who signed up to volunteer after his first visit and has since dedicated more than 300 hours of service. “The Book Thing is one of the hearts of Baltimore because books are literally just coming in, circulating into this warehouse organ and then being pumped back out, reoxygenating the literary landscape of Baltimore,” he says. “That’s its own kind of circulation, a circulation of goodwill.”

A beloved Baltimore tradition

The Book Thing of Baltimore began in 1995 when bartender Russell Wattenberg started giving away books after hearing from local teachers who came to his bar and shared that they needed books for their students. What began as a small act of generosity gradually grew into one of Baltimore’s most beloved institutions, typically held on the second weekend of the month.

In 2017, after a fire, the community came together to salvage the inventory that could be saved. The nearby Peabody Heights Brewery even put up shelves to house the titles that could be given out. Today, visitors line up for timed entry slots and receive nearly an hour to browse. Donations arrive by the thousands, according to board president Christopher Mergen. “We may get anywhere from 12,000 to 17,000 books a month as donations, and to process all of those is a really remarkable feat of engineering,” he says.

Volunteers unload boxes from trunks and pickup trucks, sort them, stamp them with the message “not for resale” and shelve them in categories. There are books on etiquette, “oddball” books, a section of large-print books and another of “teeny-tiny” books. One woman gave her whole set of Sweet Valley High books: “That’s a part of my teenage life,” she told a volunteer.

“It’s a place that just exists in spite of all the reasons that it shouldn’t exist,” says Mergen. “Baltimore has a reputation for being a bit quirky. It’s a scrappy sort of do-it-yourself type of place.”

Giving stories a second chapter

The Book Thing is in Waverly, a neighborhood that captures much of that offbeat, plucky spirit. On Saturdays, visitors drift between the nearby farmers market, brick row houses, coffee shops and independent businesses. The surrounding area has long been a place where literature matters. The Edgar Allan Poe House & Museum, a national historic landmark, is just a few miles away. Journalist and essayist H.L. Mencken chronicled his life in Baltimore, and F. Scott Fitzgerald lived there for several years in the 1930s.

On one giveaway day, volunteers stationed at the entrance greeted arriving patrons by clapping and dancing as they walked through the door. A visually impaired woman arrived with a friend, planning to wait outside while her companion browsed. Volunteers saw her, searched the media section and were delighted to discover an audiobook on CD that she had been interested in.

Another visitor arrived on a donation day with books from her late mother’s estate. As volunteers counted the donations, she asked if they would truly reach people who wanted them. Then, with tears in her eyes, she explained how much it meant to know that her mother’s library would find a new home.

“The Book Thing doesn’t discriminate. It sees value in all books and all people. Sometimes you go just for fun; sometimes you look for something specific; sometimes you go to meet other people who love books as much as you do,” says Baltimore native Violet LeVoit, who nominated it. “In a world where everything is monetized and every little scrap of human existence has a dollar sign attached to it, this is a place where the books are free, but the people are free too.”

A sanctuary for book lovers and storytellers

For Devina Bhalla, a local English teacher, the greatest experience she had at The Book Thing wasn’t simply finding a great read. When she first moved to the area and barely knew anyone, a fellow teacher told her it was the “most special thing about Baltimore.” And so the literary hub became one of the first places where she felt ­connected—not only to reading, but to Baltimore itself.

She introduced her boyfriend, Colin Kennedy, to the place, and the two often went together. Last year, on one of their visits, he got down on one knee and proposed right there in front of the shelves. Nobody who knew the couple was surprised. “One of my most favorite things was how many people in my life were like, ‘Oh, it’s just so right that Colin proposed there,’ ” she says.

Stories like that are why people talk about The Book Thing not merely as a book warehouse or a free store. They talk about friendship, belonging and generosity. Bhalla puts it this way: “If there was somebody in the world that was dis­illusioned with humanity, this would be the place you could take them to be like, ‘Humans can do some beautiful things too.’ ”

Why trust us

For more than 100 years, Reader’s Digest has been known for its heartwarming true stories and focus on community. In 2017, we launched the Nicest Places in America, an annual contest that honors kind, inspiring people making a difference in their hometowns. Readers send in nominations, and Reader’s Digest’s editorial team vets the entries and whittles them down with the help of a panel of judges. This year, the judges included Today’s Al Roker, Tuesdays with Morrie author Mitch Albom, author and podcast host Mónica Guzmán, StoryCorps CEO Sandra Clark, Today co-anchor Craig Melvin, and Molly Irani, the co-founder of Chai Pani Restaurant Group in Asheville, North Carolina, which was 2025’s Nicest Place in America. articles.title: When SNAP Ended, Portland’s Heretic Coffee Co. Stepped Up to Feed Its Neighbors
articles.content:
当波特兰的Heretic Coffee Co.宣布将免费提供早餐给任何需要的人时，志愿者咖啡师Panda Peitrok预计第二天会很忙碌，但她没想到这家仅500平方英尺的小店会挤满顾客，排队的人群从门口延伸到人行道。

店内已经是一片繁忙景象。咖啡机的嗞嗞声掩盖了交谈声。匆匆包好的玉米卷迅速递到顾客手中。年轻人和老人、文身者和穿着正式服装的人都挤在这里，接受伸出的援助之手。

"之前从来没有排队过，现在我整天都在盯着这条队伍，"Peitrok说。

Heretic创始人Josh White记得去年10月看到的那则公告，宣布为低收入家庭购买食品的联邦补助计划SNAP将于11月1日因政府停摆而被切断，这使得数百万人不得不担心如何度日。"我当时就想，'这太不合理了，'"White说。"我们卖早餐玉米卷，人们都要挨饿了，为什么不免费发放这些直到SNAP恢复呢？"

他给咖啡馆的社交媒体账号发了一条消息，邀请受SNAP影响的人来免费享用玉米卷和咖啡。仅几小时内，这条消息就传到了远超Heretic常规受众的范围，捐款金额超过1万美元。两天后的10月27日，一个大约10岁的男孩来到咖啡馆，问是否可以提前享用免费的SNAP早餐。

震惊之余，White决定立即开放这个计划。他再次发布了一条消息："没有任何孩子应该主动请求食物。波特兰，来吃饭吧。不要挨饿。"咖啡馆开门迎客，迎来了那一天的忙碌场景，Peitrok和其他志愿者咖啡师为100多位顾客提供了咖啡和玉米卷。

但Heretic的慷慨远不止于SNAP早餐计划。这家2023年成立的咖啡馆是一个非营利组织，专注于职业发展。"我们做的最主要的事情是帮助人们找到工作，"White说。Heretic的盈余收入被投入到咖啡馆中，作为对咖啡师工作感兴趣的人的实践培训场所。除了White，唯一一位全职员工是经理，负责日常运营，而志愿者们轮班工作，获得咖啡师经验，以便在其他地方找到有偿工作。

正是像Peitrok这样的志愿者咖啡师让Heretic变得与众不同。"每天早上从咖啡师那里得到的社交提振不再存在，这使得生活中少了一些欢乐，"一位36岁的老顾客，昵称T，自从免费早餐开始后就一直光顾这里，他说。

他经常在室外座位上就餐，即使是波特兰的雨天，他也会点一个培根早餐玉米卷和香草拿铁，观察咖啡馆的运作。在他看来，这远非简单的交易，而是充满感激之情的互动。

志愿者咖啡师Susan Retondo在这个空间工作了几周，她看到咖啡馆逐渐形成了自己的节奏——常客们互相打招呼，陌生人在早餐高峰时段开始交谈。"这是一个混合的场景，来自免费早餐计划的人和付费顾客在这里交织在一起，"Retondo说。

咖啡馆内的场景随时间而变化。狗狗在桌子下打瞌睡。顾客们在这里待上几小时——阅读、完成求职申请、进行Zoom面试，或者只是闲聊。有些人无家可归；有些人住在附近的经济适用房，或者在有限的收入下努力生活。"有几次，享用免费早餐的客人们几乎要哭出来了，"Retondo说。"那些因需要帮助而感到羞愧，或者几乎不敢相信我们会以这种方式提供帮助的人，让我难以忘怀。"

11月7日，SNAP在俄勒冈州恢复了，但Heretic的免费早餐计划仍在继续。超过1.2万名捐赠者筹集了大约40万美元，White将部分资金转移到相互援助组织，包括Equitable Giving Circle、Black Futures Farm和Feed'em Freedom Foundation。在高峰期，Heretic每天提供100到150份免费早餐。随着时间的推移，人数有所减少，但对White来说，这本就是目标。

"真正的胜利在于我们喂养的人越来越少，因为那些我们帮助的人已经找到了工作，现在可以自食其力了，"他说。"我们只是一座桥梁。"

超过100年来，《读者文摘》一直以感人的真实故事和社区关注闻名。2017年，我们启动了"美国最友善之地"年度评选，表彰那些在家乡做出贡献的善良和令人感动的人们。读者们提交推荐，而《读者文摘》的编辑团队对这些提名进行审查，并与评审团一起筛选。今年的评审团包括《今日秀》的Al Roker、《星期二与莫里》作者Mitch Albom、作家兼播客主持人Mónica Guzmán、StoryCorps首席执行官Sandra Clark、《今日秀》联合主持人Craig Melvin，以及Molly Irani，她是位于北卡罗来纳州阿什维尔的Chai Pani餐厅集团的联合创始人，该餐厅集团是2025年"美国最友善之地"的获奖者。我们致力于通过具有专业知识和经验的作家，并在与相关专家合作的基础上，制作高质量的内容。了解更多关于我们的团队、我们的贡献者和我们的编辑政策。

When Heretic Coffee Co. in Portland, Oregon, announced it would be giving away free breakfast to anyone who needed it, volunteer barista Panda Peitrok expected the next day to be busy. But they didn’t expect the 500-square-foot space to be bursting with customers or a line spilling out the door and down the sidewalk.

Inside, the cafe was already at full speed. Espresso machines hissing over overlapping voices. Hastily wrapped burritos handed over the counter. People young and old, some sporting tattoos and mohawks, others in their Sunday best, all packed inside to accept the helping hand that had been extended.

“There was never even a line before, and all of a sudden I was spending an entire day looking at a line,” says Peitrok.

How it all began

Heretic founder Josh White remembers the day last October when he read the announcement that SNAP, the federal program that helps low-income households buy groceries, would be cut off starting Nov. 1 during a government shutdown, leaving millions unsure how they would make ends meet. “I was like, ‘Well, that’s not right,’ ” says White. “We sell breakfast burritos, and people will be going hungry, so why not just give those away for free until SNAP is reinstated?”

He posted a message on the cafe’s social media inviting anyone affected by the SNAP cuts to come in for a free burrito and coffee. In just hours, the message spread far beyond Heretic’s usual audience, and donations topping $10,000 poured in. Two days later, on Oct. 27, a boy about 10 years old came in and asked if he could get a free SNAP breakfast early.

Horrified, White decided to open the program immediately. He posted again, saying: “No child should EVER have to ask for food. Portland, come eat. Do not go hungry.” The shop opened its doors and brought on that busy day when Peitrok and other volunteer baristas slung coffees and burritos to more than 100 people.

Brewing bright futures

But Heretic’s generosity far predates the SNAP breakfast program. Founded in 2023, the cafe is a nonprofit organization focused on workforce development. “The number-one thing we do is help people get jobs,” says White. Heretic’s surplus earnings go back into the coffee shop, which functions as an on-the-floor training experience for people interested in barista work, he says. A manager, the only salaried employee besides White, oversees operations, while volunteers rotate shifts to gain barista experience to land paying gigs elsewhere.

It’s volunteer baristas like Peitrok who help make Heretic magical. “The lack of the social pick-me-up that I always receive from baristas each morning would make the days feel a little less joyful,” says a 36-year-old regular nicknamed T, who has been visiting since free breakfast began.

He often sits on the patio—even on rainy Portland days—with a bacon breakfast burrito and a vanilla latte, watching the cafe move around him. What might seem like a transactional exchange, he says, instead feels grounded in gratitude.

A community for every story

Working in the same space week after week, volunteer barista Susan Retondo has watched the cafe develop its own rhythm—regulars greet each other, and conversations spark between strangers during a morning rush. “It’s a mix of people here for the breakfast program and paying customers,” says Retondo. “They overlap seamlessly.”

Scenes in the cafe shift by the hour. Dogs snooze under tables. Customers stay for hours—reading, completing job applications, doing Zoom interviews, just catching up. Some are unhoused; others live in nearby affordable housing or are stretching limited incomes. “There have been several times a guest has ordered the SNAP breakfast on the verge of tears,” says Retondo. “People carrying shame over needing help, or who are almost in disbelief that we’re offering what we are in the way that we are, stay with me.”

SNAP was reinstated in Oregon on Nov. 7, but Heretic’s free breakfast lives on. More than 12,000 donors have raised about $400,000, which White has partially redirected to mutual aid organizations, including Equitable Giving Circle, Black Futures Farm and the Feed’em Freedom Foundation. At its peak, Heretic served 100 to 150 free breakfasts per day. Numbers decreased with time, but to White, that was always the point.

“The win is actually feeding fewer people, because the people we were feeding were able to get jobs, and now they can feed themselves,” he says. “We’re just here to be a bridge.”

articles.title: In Charleston, Arkansas, a Strong Sense of Community Inspires Residents to Speak Up and Make a Difference
articles.content:
As you approach the little city of Charleston, Arkansas, you’ll see wide-open farm fields and modest homes before the highway becomes Main Street. Keep a good eye out, and there’s a chance you’ll also see a 50-something fellow wearing a high-visibility vest with a reacher-grabber tool in one hand and a trash bag in the other, collecting litter off the streets. His name is Parker Meador, and he is not a city employee. He keeps Charleston clean because he wants to, because he loves the place, because it makes him feel good to serve his neighbors.
“Parker is a fantastic human being,” says real estate agent and longtime resident Lacy Flanagan. “The majority of people here know him and love him for his efforts to clean up the town.” Meador started this work on an impulse one day last August while out walking with his daughter Gabrielle. He noticed a bit of trash lying around, so they filled a plastic bag with wrappers, cans and other debris.
It made him feel good, so he went out the next day and did the same thing, and soon it became a routine. Now, he logs about two hours every day, seven days a week. A year in, having dodged snakes, fire ants, traffic and wasps, he has collected around 900 bags of trash from all over—schools, parks, sports fields, streams, creeks. People honk and wave. Some stop to thank him. Some give him hugs.
“It’s never a job,” he says. “I enjoy it tremendously. It’s a great way to serve God and our community and be useful.” Feeling useful has been a lifelong struggle for Meador, who has several mental health disorders. “My life is incredibly difficult,” he says. “Just to stay alive is a daily effort. I have a very difficult time working in front of people, so I serve my family and community in other ways.”
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more of the Nicest Places in America, heartwarming stories, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
Charleston is the perfect setting for Meador’s effort. Located just 30 minutes from the Oklahoma border, it’s literally a one-stoplight town, and its Main Street is dotted with mom-and-pop shops and a simple brick courthouse. “Even though we’re just a small town, we’re very open-minded,” says Beverly Dotson, who nominated Charleston.
The city might be tiny and obscure, but it has an impressive claim to fame. Its school district was the first in the post-Confederacy South to desegregate all 12 grades after Brown v. Board of Education was decided in 1954. That same year, three years before nine brave students faced down the National Guard just two hours away in Little Rock, Charleston quietly shuttered its small school for Black students and welcomed the 11 pupils to its main institution—without resistance, press or fanfare.
“The leaders at the time were extraordinary people who had a vision and the wisdom to make it happen,” says Missy Moore, the current school superintendent. “The descendants of the people who made that decision are still part of this community and still want the same thing. We want to do right by everyone.” It was 72 years ago that the people of Charleston pulled off that groundbreaking feat. This year, they managed to pull off another one.
It began in late 2024, when the state of Arkansas abruptly announced that it had purchased 815 acres just outside Charleston to build a 3,000-bed prison. Most people in Charleston were furious: There aren’t even 3,000 people living in the city, and this plan would massively strain resources and change the city forever. Worse, nobody even bothered to consult them.
A grassroots coalition of farmers, blue-collar workers, digital nomads, educators and members of the Chickamauga Nation—called Gravel & Grit— sprang up. articles.title: Swanville, Minnesota, Made a Promise to Give Scholarships to Every Student—And Transformed Generations of Kids
articles.content:
When Brody Kircher stepped up to receive his high school diploma and head off to college, he knew that the people of Swanville, Minnesota, would have his back. The only question was exactly how many dollars they would put in his pocket.
“I expected maybe $4,000,” he says. But the actual amount Kircher received was much more than he guessed: $6,000. “This community really comes together,” he says. “They’re trying to make sure that everyone has a chance. We’re kind of spoiled, honestly. In a bigger place, they wouldn’t be able to do it for everybody.”
For graduates of Swanville High School, there’s never any suspense about who’ll get a scholarship: If you apply, you’ll get one. And in this tiny town deep in Minnesota farm country, where the class of 2026 numbered just 22 students, almost every senior applies.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more of the Nicest Places in America, heartwarming stories, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
Known as Dollars for Scholars, what started as a modest effort to help local students has evolved into a deep-rooted institution that now gives away about $100,000 in scholarships a year. Recipients can use the money for almost anything: college, trade school or continuing life skills for special education students. The program is backed by a year-round fundraising effort that includes bingo games, poinsettia sales, and weekly “meat raffles,” where locals buy chances to fill their freezers.
“Spin the wheel, and if it lands on your number, you win some meat,” says Dollars for Scholars president Teresa Giese, who nominated Swanville. “It’s a social thing. People love it. When my friends and I lose, we say, ‘It’s for the kids.’ ”
So how small is Swanville? The 2020 census counted just 326 people. Founded in 1883 as a timber town, Swanville today is a farming community best known for soybeans and the production of turkeys.
Drive through and you’ll see a cluster of homes, small businesses, grain elevators and steel storage sheds. You’ll see a bar called Lucky’s Saloon and a restaurant called Patriots Cafe that serves breakfast and lunch. You’ll see a school, a church and a little dirt road that leads to a little town dock on a little lake. Then you’ll be back in the soybean fields, on your way to the next little town.
“People say, ‘Oh, I’m from a small town; we know everybody’s name.’ I say, ‘We’re so small, we know everybody’s middle name,’ ” says Chris Kircher, Brody’s father, who chairs Swanville’s school board and owns a sporting goods store. But “small” doesn’t mean struggling. Last year, Dollars for Scholars surpassed $1 million in money awarded. Nobody imagined that kind of sustained success when a few locals launched the program in 1987, hoping to keep enrollment up and prevent the school from losing students to larger neighboring school districts.
“I was one of the first people to get a scholarship. I got it in 1991. I got $103,” says Chris. “I went to the bank, and they gave me a $100 bill and three ones.” These days, most students get at least a few thousand, and this year’s top recipient got $7,000.
The financial base is an interest-generating endowment established years ago with a $100,000 donation from the local Lions Club and buttressed by annual fundraising. The program allows local donors to create personalized scholarships, often in memory of friends and family. Those contributions are matched by the main fund, so $250 from a donor becomes $500 for a student.
“People here aren’t rich. We don’t have a lot of money. But when we need it, we find it,” says the elder Kircher.
“There were times when we were concerned that we were going to lose our school. Now we’re adding classrooms,” says Stephenie Och, whose mother helped found Dollars for Scholars.
Her son Ethan Och graduated in 2016 and won $3,000 in scholarships. That helped him stay on track in his critical first year at the University of Minnesota, providing ready cash for pesky expenses like dorm fees and books. It wasn’t the first time that Swanville stepped up for him. Spinal muscular atrophy, a rare genetic condition, had put him in a wheelchair when he was a toddler. The Lions Club helped make his home wheelchair accessible. After he started school, the community passed a referendum to upgrade the building, adding ramps and other modifications.
“They needed to modernize—it was such an old building,” says Ethan. “So they saw my situation as an opportunity, not just for me but for other students too.” Ethan got a degree in aerospace engineering and mechanics, and today is a software engineer working for one of the nation’s leading defense contractors: “My dream job,” he says. He’s also funding scholarships of his own, including one that went to Brody Kircher.
And as for Brody, he’s off at the University of Minnesota’s Morris campus, playing wide receiver. He can easily see himself coming back to Swanville someday, he says, and would recommend the town to anyone. “I liked not being a stranger to anybody,” he says. “It’s easy to get to know people. They have faith in you. They have faith in everyone.”

articles.title: A Tiny Village in New York Spread Charity Far and Wide—And Became 2026’s Nicest Place in America
articles.content:
To get the best out of a crawfish, you need to work for it: You have to twist and pull to separate the tail from the head, push the meat from the tail with your thumb, then go back and suck the flavor from the head. But getting the best out of Liverpool, New York, isn’t nearly the same squeeze. The village, only a square mile in size and 2,600 strong in population, fits right in neighboring Syracuse’s pocket. Despite its small scale, both charity and volunteerism pour from Liverpool at a disproportionate rate, making it a lily pad and vital leaping-off point for the entire region. The westerly side of town is almost entirely modest homes on shady, tree-lined streets; the easterly side is Onondaga Lake Park and small businesses with punny names (e.g., a yarn store called Knitty Gritty, a hair salon called Dead Ends). The neon filament that lights the sky at Heid’s of Liverpool, a legendary hot dog restaurant that draws crowds from miles around, serves as Liverpool’s informal welcome sign. American High, an indie film studio, moved into the old A.V. Zogg Middle School in 2017, borrowing the classrooms and Liverpool’s all-American good looks for the teen movies it produces. “Many of the suburbs of Syracuse are just that—a sprawl of homes,” says Rick Pelotte, project manager for Operation Northern Comfort, an area nonprofit born in Liverpool. “But Liverpool has a stronger identity.” One of the biggest parties of the year for the village is an annual crawfish festival, when Liverpool’s Operation Northern Comfort borrows Syracuse’s bustling Clinton Square to host more than 6,000 attendees from all over central New York. But that idyllic small-town vibe is only part of what makes Liverpool an amazing place. It also has a rich history of service that stretches back more than two decades, and its residents show up for one another in tangible, heartwarming ways. Read on to find out what makes this tiny town tick and why it earned the title of Reader’s Digest’s Nicest Place in America for 2026. Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more of the Nicest Places in America, heartwarming stories, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long. It wasn’t always called Operation Northern Comfort. When it was founded in 2005 by the late Norm “Mr. Liverpool” Andrzejewski, it was Operation Southern Comfort, an organization that sent central New Yorkers to Louisiana by the busload to help rebuild after Hurricane Katrina. Cisco Gonzales Jr. was 11 when Operation Southern Comfort helped rebuild his church in Louisiana and raise a family member’s house after the storm. He remembers the volunteers bringing supplies, extra hands, meals, and even donated tubas, trumpets and snare drums for local school bands. But more importantly, “they just brought hope,” he says. For six years, the organization made routine trips to Louisiana, equipping a class of thousands of volunteers with new building and construction knowledge. It rebranded in 2012 as Operation Northern Comfort, ready to put its volunteers’ new skills to work at home, but not without taking a bit of Louisiana with it in the crawfish festival. Today, Operation Northern Comfort primarily builds ramps and lifts that give area residents with accessibility challenges the freedom to leave the house. (“People think there’s a government agency or something that you can call, but there isn’t,” says Laurel Flanagan, CEO of Operation Northern Comfort.) But if you can dream it, they can build it: bookshelves, desks, even DJ tables. The festival, always the first Saturday in May (crawfish are no good any later), took place this year in unseasonably brisk weather, but the steam kept volunteer crawfish cooks warm as they stood over the boil. Blistering red mudbugs swirled around the pot with onions, garlic and lemon, plus a healthy serving of celery to soak up some of the Cajun spice that dyes the broth orange. Youth volunteers washed baskets of live crawfish—shrieking if one clung to their shirt—to replenish the stock. More volunteers appeared with sport fishing nets slung over their shoulders to scoop cooked mudbugs from the boil and deliver them to a preparation station. Boxes of crawfish packed with corn and potatoes disappeared from the pickup table, toted around by merry attendees as they danced to live music and snapped photos with the crawfish mascot. “I didn’t know it was a fundraiser for, like, a year,” says Flanagan, a festival attendee turned volunteer before she became CEO. Gonzales, now 32, flies up for the festival every year, often staying in the homes of old pals in Liverpool and showing attendees how to peel crawfish. “I always laugh, because if you ask my dad, he says, ‘You go there every year just to drink and have fun,’ ” says Gonzales, “and I’m like, ‘Yeah, that’s exactly what I do.’ ”
Every cent of the $40,000 raised by this year’s event will be poured directly back into the town and its neighbors. Festival revenue is the source of nearly all the money that Operation Northern Comfort raises each year, powering the 57 projects it completed in 2025. But Operation Northern Comfort is just one piston in Liverpool’s charitable engine. “I nominated Liverpool because there are so many things that end up in our news of individuals who spend their time, their effort, to help other people,” says Liverpool resident Susan Edmonds, who herself volunteers at both the Humane Society and the airport military courtesy room. “If you think an individual doesn’t make a difference, boy that’s wrong.”
Ralph Rotella moved to Liverpool from Syracuse 31 years ago, after having arrived in the country in 1970. The village offers a bit of space between him and the city, and more room for a garden. Around the back of his house, you’ll find the tomatoes, cucumbers and zucchinis he tends with any free time he can eke out. On the doorstep, there’s a good chance you’ll find a garbage bag full of shoes. Rotella is a cobbler, a trade that the Italian immigrant inherited from his uncle, along with his shop, Discount Shoe Repair in downtown Syracuse. Every year, the Liverpool resident gives away thousands of refurbished shoes to the Syracuse Rescue Mission so they can find the feet of someone who needs them. Donations come in all forms (boots, sneakers, dress shoes, loafers), sometimes by the bag, sometimes a pair at a time. Occasionally, someone will buy and donate a new pair of shoes just to support the cobbler’s cause and save him the work of fixing heels, replacing laces or restoring soles. “The first year, I was so excited—we got 35 pairs. After the third year, a few hundred pairs. Now, every day, you see how many we got,” Rotella says, gesturing at the shoe-filled trash bags in his shop’s entryway. “That pile is only a week old. We almost got 500 pairs.”
Every day, at least a few people drop by the shop to add to the mountain of shoes—and some drop them off at Rotella’s doorstep in Liverpool. The Rescue Mission makes a pickup every three weeks so Discount Shoe Repair won’t get totally overrun. “I could never do it by myself,” says Rotella of the thousands of donors who make it possible. “Thanks to you guys and thanks to me, we do a good deed.”
Last December, when the Rescue Mission backed its truck up to Discount Shoe Repair’s doors for the final pickup of the year, the shoe drive made a new one-year record of more than 45,000 pairs. It’s always a celebration, complete with roasting chestnuts and jaunty Italian music, but this was a special milestone—300,000 pairs collected since Rotella started the drive in 2011. “I reached my goal, but I’m still going to do it no matter what,” he says. “As long as my hands work and I can walk and dance, we’ll do it. I’ve been in Liverpool since 1995, and anyplace I go, in the grocery store or Home Depot, they say, ‘Ralph, I got some shoes for you. Can I bring them down?’ ”
The Rev. Bruce Gowe hasn’t lived in Liverpool for nearly as long as Rotella, but it didn’t take long for the village to reveal itself to him. He moved to Liverpool about two years ago, when he started his ministry at St. Matthew’s Episcopal Church, a simple redbrick building on Liverpool’s outskirts near the highway that borders the village on the opposite side from Onondaga Lake. Lots of the offerings in the region appeal to Gowe: hiking the Finger Lakes, the boisterous festival seasons, a community that cares for nature. He’s among the younger priests that staff the area’s 22 churches of varying denominations, and the first openly gay one at St. Matthew’s. The congregation, and Liverpool, embraced him with ease, an openness that he sees extending well beyond himself. “There’s a sense of community and safety; you can thrive here,” says Gowe. “There’s that sense of being a large city, but there’s also the small-town America feel too.” Last August, Gowe noticed a woman using one of the church’s outdoor outlets to charge her phone in the parking lot. He’d seen her once before, pushing a shopping cart a bit up the road, and realized she must be homeless and had likely set up camp in the woods behind St. Matthew’s. Gowe didn’t mind—he said hello and told her that any time the church doors are open, she’s welcome to come inside. “The Scripture says you never know when you’re hosting angels,” he says. In time, a few members of the congregation built a rapport with the woman, until she eventually felt comfortable resting in the shade of the entryway and coming inside for a cup of coffee. St. Matthew’s supports local food pantries and also runs its own, and a care team began regularly preparing a special basket to help her get through the week. There’s a shower in the church building—they asked if she would like to come in and use it? One churchgoer offered to take the occasional load of laundry home for her, until another found a donated washer and dryer to install at the church. By fall, she was donning a Halloween mask for the trunk-or-treat event. Gowe decided to contact In My Father’s Kitchen, a nonprofit in Syracuse offering direct street outreach to people experiencing homelessness, after hearing about it from another parish. Upon meeting the woman, co-founder John Tumino realized he’d met her before and had been trying to get her into housing for months before she disappeared to Liverpool. Today, she’s in an apartment in Syracuse thanks to Tumino—and the relationships she built in Liverpool. “Being part of the community allowed her to make those steps forward of ‘Maybe I do need help, and maybe there are folks who are safe enough for me to take that step,’ ” says Gowe. “I don’t think this would happen at other places—certainly at other places in Liverpool, but not necessarily other places in the country.”
“In a time where everyone is looking straight ahead and just taking care of themselves, it’s nice to know that if I get in trouble, I can knock next door and there’s someone there that’ll open the door and smile,” says Liverpool resident Simone McCarthy. “And that’s what Liverpool is.” Or, as 31-year-old Kenyan immigrant Raiss Muya puts it, “What makes Liverpool, Liverpool, is the people.”
Muya is the “someone next door” McCarthy was referring to—he has been her neighbor since he was 17. His kids call her Grandma, just as he used to, and spend hot summer days swimming in her above-ground pool. His parents have since gone back to Kenya and his siblings have moved out of state, but he took over the family home, unable to imagine life away from the village that welcomed him. “Once we got here, everyone around just helped us out. We told ourselves, ‘This is the place to be,’ ” recalls Muya.

“他们向我们伸出了援手”
当几年前的一场暴风雪摧毁了穆雅和麦卡锡家之间的围栏，使麦卡锡凹陷的车道暴露在难以清理的漫天飞雪中时，麦卡锡几乎不需要开口，穆雅就伸出了援手。他挖出了被积雪和冰层掩埋的旧围栏，用铁丝将栅栏固定在柱子上作为临时修复，直到春天。几个月后，麦卡锡的房东出资购买材料，穆雅这位手艺人在繁忙的工作之余，带着自己的两个小女儿，在傍晚时分修建了一道6英尺高的雪松围栏，以阻挡来年冬季的积雪。两个小女孩虽然更爱玩耍铲子而非挖坑，但也帮着持平尺和为父亲取水。穆雅说：“她对我们照顾得无微不至。我为什么要拒绝，甚至需要考虑呢？”

麦卡锡经常带着饼干和额外的饭菜来到穆雅家送给他们，因为她常常做得太多。她说：“食物的最佳储存地就是邻居的肚子里。”至今，她还从锡拉丘兹的CNY Blessing Box食物银行带回食物、干货和符合哈拉尔标准的鸡肉，那里她是一名志愿者。这并非他们请求，而是她认为“这是该做的事”。

“如果你们的小镇有新邻居，去看看他们吧。”穆雅说，“他们会让你惊喜——因为西蒙娜确实让我们惊喜了。”
“你不需要去拯救世界。”麦卡锡说，“只要拯救你的街区。”

利物浦镇长斯泰西·芬尼（Stacy Finney）同时是一名公立学校的美术教师，她认为小镇的居民并未意识到他们的生活多么特别。她记得一位朋友经过此地前往芝加哥时，惊叹于在奥奈达湖公园玩耍的孩子和其他镇民，他们看起来多么幸福和无忧无虑。他说：“他们似乎认为这种生活再正常不过。”芬尼说：“确实如此，他们确实这样认为。”

那天，他们在奥奈达湖骑行。莫霍克、奥奈达、卡尤加和塞尼卡人曾在此岸缔结和平，使之成为一片神圣之地。20世纪初期的工业污染使奥奈达湖一度成为美国最严重污染的湖泊之一，但经过艰苦努力，现在这里又能钓鱼了，鸟类爱好者也纷纷前来拍摄位于斯卡诺赫（Skä•noñh）大法和平中心附近的雄鹰巢穴。

芬尼补充道：“我认为利物浦确实有一种志愿精神。因为人们热爱他们生活的地方，他们希望能让其更美好。你必须热爱你生活的地方，并在这里投入时间。”

超过一个世纪以来，读者文摘以温馨的真实故事和对社区的关注而闻名。2017年，我们启动了“美国最友善的地方”年度评选活动，旨在表彰那些在家乡做出贡献、值得尊敬和鼓舞的人们。读者提名候选人，读者文摘编辑团队在评委团的帮助下评审并缩减候选人名单。今年的评委包括《今日美国》的艾尔·罗克、《与莫里周二聊天》作者米奇·阿尔邦、作家兼播客主持人莫妮卡·古兹曼、StoryCorps首席执行官桑德拉·克拉克、《今日美国》主播克雷格·梅尔文以及今年的最佳友善之地亚什维尔市Chai Pani餐饮集团的联合创始人莫莉·伊拉尼。我们致力于由具备专业知识和经验的作家与相关合格专家合作，制作高质量的内容。请阅读更多关于我们团队、贡献者和编辑政策的内容。本文《纽约州一座小镇传播慈善——成为2026年美国最友善的地方》首次发表于读者文摘。
articles.summary:
To get the best out of a crawfish, you need to work for it: You have to twist and pull to separate the tail from the head, push the meat from the tail with your thumb, then go back and suck the flavor from the head. But getting the best out of Liverpool, New York, isn’t nearly the same squeeze.

The village, only a square mile in size and 2,600 strong in population, fits right in neighboring Syracuse’s pocket. Despite its small scale, both charity and volunteerism pour from Liverpool at a disproportionate rate, making it a lily pad and vital leaping-off point for the entire region. The westerly side of town is almost entirely modest homes on shady, tree-lined streets; the easterly side is Onondaga Lake Park and small businesses with punny names (e.g., a yarn store called Knitty Gritty, a hair salon called Dead Ends).

The neon filament that lights the sky at Heid’s of Liverpool, a legendary hot dog restaurant that draws crowds from miles around, serves as Liverpool’s informal welcome sign. American High, an indie film studio, moved into the old A.V. Zogg Middle School in 2017, borrowing the classrooms and Liverpool’s all-American good looks for the teen movies it produces.

“Many of the suburbs of Syracuse are just that—a sprawl of homes,” says Rick Pelotte, project manager for Operation Northern Comfort, an area nonprofit born in Liverpool. “But Liverpool has a stronger identity.” One of the biggest parties of the year for the village is an annual crawfish festival, when Liverpool’s Operation Northern Comfort borrows Syracuse’s bustling Clinton Square to host more than 6,000 attendees from all over central New York.

But that idyllic small-town vibe is only part of what makes Liverpool an amazing place. It also has a rich history of service that stretches back more than two decades, and its residents show up for one another in tangible, heartwarming ways. Read on to find out what makes this tiny town tick and why it earned the title of Reader’s Digest’s Nicest Place in America for 2026.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more of the Nicest Places in America, heartwarming stories, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long. 

Inside Operation Northern Comfort

It wasn’t always called Operation Northern Comfort. When it was founded in 2005 by the late Norm “Mr. Liverpool” Andrzejewski, it was Operation Southern Comfort, an organization that sent central New Yorkers to Louisiana by the busload to help rebuild after Hurricane Katrina. Cisco Gonzales Jr. was 11 when Operation Southern Comfort helped rebuild his church in Louisiana and raise a family member’s house after the storm. He remembers the volunteers bringing supplies, extra hands, meals, and even donated tubas, trumpets and snare drums for local school bands. But more importantly, “they just brought hope,” he says.

For six years, the organization made routine trips to Louisiana, equipping a class of thousands of volunteers with new building and construction knowledge. It rebranded in 2012 as Operation Northern Comfort, ready to put its volunteers’ new skills to work at home, but not without taking a bit of Louisiana with it in the crawfish festival. Today, Operation Northern Comfort primarily builds ramps and lifts that give area residents with accessibility challenges the freedom to leave the house. (“People think there’s a government agency or something that you can call, but there isn’t,” says Laurel Flanagan, CEO of Operation Northern Comfort.) But if you can dream it, they can build it: bookshelves, desks, even DJ tables.

The festival, always the first Saturday in May (crawfish are no good any later), took place this year in unseasonably brisk weather, but the steam kept volunteer crawfish cooks warm as they stood over the boil. Blistering red mudbugs swirled around the pot with onions, garlic and lemon, plus a healthy serving of celery to soak up some of the Cajun spice that dyes the broth orange. Youth volunteers washed baskets of live crawfish—shrieking if one clung to their shirt—to replenish the stock.

More volunteers appeared with sport fishing nets slung over their shoulders to scoop cooked mudbugs from the boil and deliver them to a preparation station. Boxes of crawfish packed with corn and potatoes disappeared from the pickup table, toted around by merry attendees as they danced to live music and snapped photos with the crawfish mascot.

“I didn’t know it was a fundraiser for, like, a year,” says Flanagan, a festival attendee turned volunteer before she became CEO. Gonzales, now 32, flies up for the festival every year, often staying in the homes of old pals in Liverpool and showing attendees how to peel crawfish. “I always laugh, because if you ask my dad, he says, ‘You go there every year just to drink and have fun,’ ” says Gonzales, “and I’m like, ‘Yeah, that’s exactly what I do.’ ”

Every cent of the $40,000 raised by this year’s event will be poured directly back into the town and its neighbors. Festival revenue is the source of nearly all the money that Operation Northern Comfort raises each year, powering the 57 projects it completed in 2025. But Operation Northern Comfort is just one piston in Liverpool’s charitable engine.

“I nominated Liverpool because there are so many things that end up in our news of individuals who spend their time, their effort, to help other people,” says Liverpool resident Susan Edmonds, who herself volunteers at both the Humane Society and the airport military courtesy room. “If you think an individual doesn’t make a difference, boy that’s wrong.”

An individual difference

Ralph Rotella moved to Liverpool from Syracuse 31 years ago, after having arrived in the country in 1970. The village offers a bit of space between him and the city, and more room for a garden. Around the back of his house, you’ll find the tomatoes, cucumbers and zucchinis he tends with any free time he can eke out. On the doorstep, there’s a good chance you’ll find a garbage bag full of shoes.

Rotella is a cobbler, a trade that the Italian immigrant inherited from his uncle, along with his shop, Discount Shoe Repair in downtown Syracuse. Every year, the Liverpool resident gives away thousands of refurbished shoes to the Syracuse Rescue Mission so they can find the feet of someone who needs them.

Donations come in all forms (boots, sneakers, dress shoes, loafers), sometimes by the bag, sometimes a pair at a time. Occasionally, someone will buy and donate a new pair of shoes just to support the cobbler’s cause and save him the work of fixing heels, replacing laces or restoring soles. “The first year, I was so excited—we got 35 pairs. After the third year, a few hundred pairs. Now, every day, you see how many we got,” Rotella says, gesturing at the shoe-filled trash bags in his shop’s entryway. “That pile is only a week old. We almost got 500 pairs.”

Every day, at least a few people drop by the shop to add to the mountain of shoes—and some drop them off at Rotella’s doorstep in Liverpool. The Rescue Mission makes a pickup every three weeks so Discount Shoe Repair won’t get totally overrun. “I could never do it by myself,” says Rotella of the thousands of donors who make it possible. “Thanks to you guys and thanks to me, we do a good deed.”

Last December, when the Rescue Mission backed its truck up to Discount Shoe Repair’s doors for the final pickup of the year, the shoe drive made a new one-year record of more than 45,000 pairs. It’s always a celebration, complete with roasting chestnuts and jaunty Italian music, but this was a special milestone—300,000 pairs collected since Rotella started the drive in 2011.

“I reached my goal, but I’m still going to do it no matter what,” he says. “As long as my hands work and I can walk and dance, we’ll do it. I’ve been in Liverpool since 1995, and anyplace I go, in the grocery store or Home Depot, they say, ‘Ralph, I got some shoes for you. Can I bring them down?’ ”

“If the doors are open, you are welcome here”

The Rev. Bruce Gowe hasn’t lived in Liver­pool for nearly as long as Rotella, but it didn’t take long for the village to reveal itself to him. He moved to Liverpool about two years ago, when he started his ministry at St. Matthew’s Episcopal Church, a simple redbrick building on Liverpool’s outskirts near the highway that borders the village on the opposite side from Onondaga Lake.

Lots of the offerings in the region appeal to Gowe: hiking the Finger Lakes, the boisterous festival seasons, a community that cares for nature. He’s among the younger priests that staff the area’s 22 churches of varying denominations, and the first openly gay one at St. Matthew’s. The congregation, and Liverpool, embraced him with ease, an openness that he sees extending well beyond himself.

“There’s a sense of community and safety; you can thrive here,” says Gowe. “There’s that sense of being a large city, but there’s also the small-town America feel too.” Last August, Gowe noticed a woman using one of the church’s outdoor outlets to charge her phone in the parking lot. He’d seen her once before, pushing a shopping cart a bit up the road, and realized she must be homeless and had likely set up camp in the woods behind St. Matthew’s. Gowe didn’t mind—he said hello and told her that any time the church doors are open, she’s welcome to come inside.

“The Scripture says you never know when you’re hosting angels,” he says.

In time, a few members of the congregation built a rapport with the woman, until she eventually felt comfortable resting in the shade of the entryway and coming inside for a cup of coffee. St. Matthew’s supports local food pantries and also runs its own, and a care team began regularly preparing a special basket to help her get through the week. There’s a shower in the church building—they asked if she would like to come in and use it? One churchgoer offered to take the occasional load of laundry home for her, until another found a donated washer and dryer to install at the church. By fall, she was donning a Halloween mask for the trunk-or-treat event.

Gowe decided to contact In My Father’s Kitchen, a nonprofit in Syracuse offering direct street outreach to people experiencing homelessness, after hearing about it from another parish. Upon meeting the woman, co-founder John Tumino realized he’d met her before and had been trying to get her into housing for months before she disappeared to Liverpool. Today, she’s in an apartment in ­Syracuse thanks to Tumino—and the relationships she built in Liverpool. “Being part of the community ­allowed her to make those steps forward of ‘Maybe I do need help, and maybe there are folks who are safe enough for me to take that step,’ ” says Gowe. “I don’t think this would happen at other places—certainly at other places in Liverpool, but not necessarily other places in the country.”

What makes a village

“In a time where everyone is looking straight ahead and just taking care of themselves, it’s nice to know that if I get in trouble, I can knock next door and there’s someone there that’ll open the door and smile,” says Liverpool resident Simone McCarthy. “And that’s what Liverpool is.” Or, as 31-year-old Kenyan immigrant Raiss Muya puts it, “What makes Liverpool, Liverpool, is the people.”

Muya is the “someone next door” McCarthy was referring to—he has been her neighbor since he was 17. His kids call her Grandma, just as he used to, and spend hot summer days swimming in her above-ground pool. His parents have since gone back to Kenya and his siblings have moved out of state, but he took over the family home, unable to imagine life away from the village that welcomed him.

“Once we got here, everyone around just helped us out. We told ourselves, ‘This is the place to be,’ ” recalls Muya. “They had their hands open for us.”

So when a blizzard demolished the fence between his and McCarthy’s properties a few winters back, leaving her recessed driveway exposed to snow that would drift in and be impossible to clear, she barely had to ask before Muya opened his own hand.

He dug up the old fence, which was buried beneath mounds of snow and ice, and tethered the panels to the posts with wire as a temporary fix until spring. A few months later, McCar­thy’s landlord ponied up for the supplies, and Muya, a handyman, built a 6-foot cedar fence to block the following years’ snowfall. He worked in the evenings, after long days of fixing up other people’s homes, with the help of his young daughters, who did more wrestling with the shovel than digging post holes but held the level and fetched water for him.

“She helped us with everything. There’s no reason why I should say no or even think about it, you know?” says Muya. McCarthy often stops over with cookies and extra meals for the Muyas when she cooks too much. (“The best place to store food is in your neighbor’s stomach,” she’ll tell you.) To this day, she brings home groceries, dry goods and halal chicken, from the CNY Blessing Box, a food pantry in Syracuse where she volunteers. Not because they asked, but because, she says, “It’s the right thing to do.”

“If you have new neighbors in your town, go see what they’re about,” says Muya. “They’ll surprise you—because Simone definitely surprised us.”

“You don’t have to go out and save the world,” says McCarthy. “Just save your block.”

Block by block

Stacy Finney, Liverpool’s mayor and a public school art teacher, doesn’t think most people in town realize how special the place is. She remembers a friend passing through on his way to Chicago, and the way he marveled at their kids and other townsfolk, blissful and carefree at Onondaga Lake Park.

“He was like, ‘Look at them thinking this is totally normal.’ And it was true, you know, they do,” she says. “They genuinely think that this is normal.”

They were biking that day along Onondaga Lake, on whose shores the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca people once brokered peace, making it a sacred space to be respected. Decades of industrial dumping at the turn of the 20th century rendered Onondaga one of the most polluted lakes in the country, but tremendous effort has made it fishable again, and birders flock to photograph the eagle’s nest near the Skä•noñh Great Law of Peace Center.

“I do think there’s a spirit of volunteerism in Liverpool,” Finney continues. “Because people love the area they live in, they want to enhance it. You’ve got to love where you live, and invest your time where you live.”

Why trust us

For more than 100 years, Reader’s Digest has been known for its heartwarming true stories and focus on community. In 2017, we launched the Nicest Places in America, an annual contest that honors kind, inspiring people making a difference in their hometowns. Readers send in nominations, and Reader’s Digest’s editorial team vets the entries and whittles them down with the help of a panel of judges. This year, the judges included Today’s Al Roker, Tuesdays with Morrie author Mitch Albom, author and podcast host Mónica Guzmán, StoryCorps CEO Sandra Clark, Today co-anchor Craig Melvin, and Molly Irani, the co-founder of Chai Pani Restaurant Group in Asheville, NC, which was 2025’s Nicest Place in America.
